question:
A data scientist at PharmaGen Research is using SageMaker Script Mode to train a machine learning model for predicting compound bioactivity.

The team needs to modularize their codebase by separating model definition, training logic, and inference logic into distinct Python files.

The solution must also support the installation of several external third-party dependencies that are not included in the base SageMaker container image.

How should the data scientist proceed to ensure SageMaker can correctly discover and execute the custom model code, while keeping operational overhead to a minimum?
options: Use SageMaker's built-in algorithms and ignore the need for custom modularized code.
Build a custom Docker container that bundles all Python files and dependencies, push it to Amazon ECR, and reference it in the SageMaker estimator as a custom image URI.
Consolidate all logic into a single Python script and embed dependency installation calls using subprocess or pip directly within the script at runtime.

Split the code into multiple Python files, package them together, and specify a single entry point script in the SageMaker estimator. Use a requirements.txt file to declare and install the external dependencies.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SageMaker Script Mode for custom training code.

It focuses on using source_dir, entry_point, and requirements.txt to support a modular Python codebase with external dependencies while avoiding custom container overhead.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Use SageMaker's built-in algorithms and ignore the need for custom modularized code: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms use predefined algorithm logic. They are not the right choice when the scenario requires custom modular Python code and third-party dependencies.

Split the code into multiple Python files, package them together, and specify a single entry point script in the SageMaker estimator. Use a requirements.txt file to declare and install the external dependencies: This is the correct option. Amazon SageMaker Script Mode supports modular code through source_dir and a single entry_point script. Dependencies can be declared in requirements.txt.

Build a custom Docker container that bundles all Python files and dependencies, push it to Amazon ECR, and reference it in the SageMaker estimator as a custom image URI: This option is valid in more advanced scenarios, but it is unnecessary here. A custom container adds operational overhead, including Dockerfile maintenance, image builds, Amazon ECR management, and patching.

Consolidate all logic into a single Python script and embed dependency installation calls using subprocess or pip directly within the script at runtime: This option is incorrect. Collapsing all logic into one file breaks modular design, and installing packages with runtime pip calls inside the script is fragile and not the recommended Amazon SageMaker pattern.

Why source_dir, entry_point, and requirements.txt fit this scenario.

The scenario requires custom training code.

The codebase is modular.

The project has multiple Python files.

The training job also needs external dependencies.

The team wants minimal operational overhead.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker Script Mode.

In Script Mode, the team defines a source directory using source_dir.

That directory can contain multiple Python modules, helper files, and dependency definitions.

The team then specifies one training launcher script using entry_point.

When the training job starts, Amazon SageMaker packages the source directory, uploads it, and makes it available inside the managed framework container.

If a requirements.txt file is included, dependencies can be installed before the training script runs.

This avoids building a custom Docker image.

It also avoids managing image lifecycle in Amazon ECR.

Custom containers are still useful when the workload requires OS-level packages, unsupported frameworks, custom CUDA versions, or specialized runtime environments.

But for modular Python training code with Python package dependencies, Script Mode is the lower-overhead answer.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Modular Python code: Use source_dir.

Single training launcher: Use entry_point.

External dependencies: Declare packages in requirements.txt.

Managed framework container: Avoid custom container maintenance.

Minimal operational overhead: Avoid unnecessary Amazon ECR workflows.

SageMaker-native training: Keep the workflow inside managed Amazon SageMaker training jobs.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Script Mode + multiple Python files + external dependencies + minimal overhead = source_dir + entry_point + requirements.txt.

Remember:

source_dir: Directory containing the training project files.

entry_point: Main script executed by the training job.

requirements.txt: Declares Python package dependencies.

Managed framework containers: Supported containers maintained by AWS.

Custom Docker container: Use only when the environment needs deeper customization.

Amazon ECR: Required for custom container images, not for standard Script Mode.

Built-in algorithms: Good for predefined algorithms, not custom modular training code.

Official AWS references.

Use the SageMaker Training Toolkit.

Key exam terms: Amazon SageMaker Script Mode, source_dir, entry_point, requirements.txt, managed framework containers, custom Docker container, Amazon ECR, operational overhead, modular Python codebase, external dependencies.

question:
A data scientist at an aerospace and defense contractor, OrbitShield Systems, is building an anomaly detection model using Amazon SageMaker to identify defective components in manufacturing sensor data.

The dataset is highly imbalanced, with only 2% of the records representing defective components.

The scientist wants to ensure the model can effectively detect defects while minimizing false negatives. Which techniques should the scientist use to handle this issue? (Select TWO.)
options: Perform dimensionality reduction to reduce the number of features and make the dataset more manageable.
Use Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning (AMT) with a Recall objective metric to optimize the model's sensitivity toward the minority class.
Train the model on the original imbalanced dataset and rely solely on accuracy as the evaluation metric to determine model quality.
Use weighted loss functions during training to penalize misclassification of the minority class.
Use oversampling techniques, such as SMOTE, to balance the dataset before training.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests how to handle severe class imbalance in binary classification problems.

It focuses on selecting training-time strategies that improve detection of a critical minority class and reduce false negatives.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Perform dimensionality reduction to reduce the number of features and make the dataset more manageable: This option is incorrect. Dimensionality reduction reduces feature count, but it does not fix class imbalance. It may even remove useful signal related to the minority class.

Use Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with a Recall objective metric to optimize the model's sensitivity toward the minority class: This option is useful but incomplete. Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning can optimize hyperparameters using metrics such as Recall, but it does not rebalance the dataset or change the loss function by itself. It is complementary, not sufficient as the primary imbalance solution.

Use oversampling techniques, such as SMOTE, to balance the dataset before training: This is a correct option. SMOTE and other oversampling techniques increase the representation of the minority class in the training data. This helps the model learn decision boundaries for rare but important positive cases.

Use weighted loss functions during training to penalize misclassification of the minority class: This is a correct option. Weighted loss functions make mistakes on the minority class more expensive during training. This encourages the model to pay more attention to rare positive cases.

Train the model on the original imbalanced dataset and rely solely on accuracy as the evaluation metric to determine model quality: This option is incorrect. Accuracy is misleading on heavily imbalanced datasets. A model can achieve high accuracy by predicting the majority class while failing to detect the minority class.

Why SMOTE and weighted loss functions fit this scenario.

The dataset is highly imbalanced.

The minority class is important.

False negatives are costly.

That means the model must be trained to pay more attention to rare positive examples.

Two strong training-time strategies address this directly.

The first is oversampling.

Oversampling increases the number of minority-class examples in the training set.

SMOTE creates synthetic minority-class samples, helping the model see more examples of the rare class during training.

The second is weighted loss.

Weighted loss functions assign a higher penalty to mistakes on the minority class.

This changes the optimization objective so the model does not ignore rare positive cases.

These strategies are stronger than simply changing the evaluation metric.

They also address the root cause more directly than dimensionality reduction or generic hyperparameter tuning alone.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Severe class imbalance: Use oversampling or class weighting.

Minority class detection: Increase sensitivity to rare positive cases.

False-negative reduction: Penalize missed minority-class examples.

Training-time correction: Modify the dataset distribution or loss function.

Better evaluation: Use metrics such as Recall, F1-score, or Precision-Recall AUC.

Avoid accuracy traps: Do not rely on accuracy for skewed datasets.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Imbalanced binary classification + high cost of false negatives = oversampling and weighted loss functions.

Remember:

SMOTE: Synthetic minority oversampling technique.

Oversampling: Increases minority-class representation before training.

Weighted loss function: Penalizes minority-class mistakes more heavily.

Recall: Important when false negatives are costly.

Precision-Recall AUC: Useful for imbalanced classification.

Accuracy: Often misleading with severe imbalance.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning: Helpful for tuning, but not a standalone imbalance fix.

Official AWS references.

Amazon SageMaker XGBoost hyperparameters.

Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning.

Key exam terms: class imbalance, SMOTE, oversampling, weighted loss function, minority class, false negatives, Recall objective, Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning, Precision-Recall AUC, accuracy antipattern.

question:
A maritime shipping company, OceanRoute Logistics, is building a cargo anomaly detection system to monitor vessel telemetry and port transaction data in real time.

The engineering team plans to use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the telemetry feed and requires the system to scale automatically based on demand.

Low latency is a critical requirement to enable fast anomaly detection responses, and multiple independent consumer applications  including an ML scoring endpoint, a rule-based alerting service, and a compliance auditing pipeline

must process the same stream simultaneously without competing for throughput. Which feature of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams should OceanRoute Logistics implement to best meet these requirements?
options: Use enhanced fan-out to provide dedicated throughput per consumer and reduce end-to-end consumer latency.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to automatically scale the stream and route data to downstream processing services.
Enable on-demand mode and manually scale shards based on observed throughput requirements.
Enable provisioned mode and dynamically add shards as demand increases.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests understanding of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams consumer throughput models for real-time ML pipelines.

It focuses on choosing enhanced fan-out when multiple independent consumers need low-latency access to the same stream without competing for shared read throughput.

It is tied to the Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML) domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Enable provisioned mode and dynamically add shards as demand increases: This option is incorrect. Provisioned mode can increase stream capacity through shard scaling, but standard consumers still share per-shard read throughput through GetRecords. This does not solve read contention across multiple independent consumers.

Use enhanced fan-out to provide dedicated throughput per consumer and reduce end-to-end consumer latency: This is the correct option. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer dedicated read throughput per shard and uses a push-based delivery model, reducing latency for independent real-time consumers.

Enable on-demand mode and manually scale shards based on observed throughput requirements: This option is incorrect. On-demand mode automatically scales stream capacity, but it does not by itself provide dedicated read throughput per consumer. It solves producer/stream scaling concerns, not the multi-consumer read contention problem.

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to automatically scale the stream and route data to downstream processing services: This option is incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for delivery to destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon OpenSearch Service. It is not the right service for low-latency, multi-consumer stream processing.

Why enhanced fan-out fits this scenario.

The scenario requires real-time stream consumption.

There are multiple independent consumers.

Each consumer must process the same data with low latency.

That points directly to enhanced fan-out in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

With standard consumers, applications use GetRecords.

Those consumers share the available read throughput for each shard.

As more consumers read from the same stream, they compete for throughput.

That increases latency and can create bottlenecks.

Enhanced fan-out changes this model.

Each registered enhanced fan-out consumer receives dedicated read throughput per shard.

It also uses a push-based delivery model over HTTP/2.

This is a strong fit for real-time ML inference pipelines where an anomaly detection model, rules engine, audit pipeline, or compliance processor all need to consume the same stream independently.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Multiple independent consumers: Use enhanced fan-out.

Low-latency consumption: Avoid shared polling contention.

Dedicated read throughput: Give each consumer its own per-shard throughput allocation.

Real-time ML inference: Support fast delivery to scoring or anomaly detection systems.

Avoid service mismatch: Do not replace stream processing with Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose.

Separate scaling concepts: Do not confuse on-demand mode with enhanced fan-out.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Real-time stream + multiple independent consumers + low latency = enhanced fan-out.

Remember:

Enhanced fan-out: Dedicated throughput per registered consumer.

GetRecords: Standard shared polling model.

Shared throughput: Can create contention when several consumers read from the same shard.

HTTP/2 push delivery: Used by enhanced fan-out consumers.

On-demand mode: Helps with stream capacity scaling, not per-consumer read isolation.

Provisioned mode: Requires shard capacity planning.

Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose: Delivery service, not a low-latency multi-consumer stream processing layer.

Official AWS references.

Develop enhanced fan-out consumers for Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

Key exam terms: enhanced fan-out, dedicated throughput per consumer, HTTP/2 push-based delivery, GetRecords shared polling, on-demand mode, provisioned mode, multiple independent consumers, real-time ML inference latency.

question:
A consumer electronics manufacturer, NexaGadget, needs to build a recommendation engine using a machine learning model trained on customer activity data, including purchase history, browsing patterns, and account demographics.

The team wants to streamline their model development process by creating a centralized repository of preprocessed features that can be reused across different projects.

The system must support both real-time product recommendations and scheduled batch training jobs, while ensuring feature consistency between training and inference to avoid training-serving skew.

What is the MOST appropriate setup for the team to ensure consistent feature reuse, while also optimizing for real-time and batch processing?
options: Use Amazon DynamoDB as a centralized feature repository, storing precomputed features for low-latency real-time access, and export snapshots to Amazon S3 for batch training.
Use SageMaker Feature Store to create an offline store for batch training and an online store for real-time inference.
Store all features in Amazon S3 and manually preprocess them for each model training run, using AWS Glue jobs to enforce schema consistency across projects.
Use SageMaker Feature Store to create an online store for batch processing and an offline store for real-time recommendations.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SageMaker Feature Store and its dual-store architecture.

It focuses on using the offline store for batch training and the online store for low-latency real-time inference while keeping feature definitions consistent across ML workflows.

It is tied to the Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML) domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Store all features in Amazon S3 and manually preprocess them for each model training run, using AWS Glue jobs to enforce schema consistency across projects: This option is incorrect. Amazon S3 and AWS Glue can support data preparation workflows, but manually managing features across projects creates operational overhead and increases the risk of training-serving skew.

Use SageMaker Feature Store to create an offline store for batch training and an online store for real-time inference: This is the correct option. Amazon SageMaker Feature Store provides an offline store for historical batch training data and an online store for low-latency feature retrieval during real-time inference.

Use SageMaker Feature Store to create an online store for batch processing and an offline store for real-time recommendations: This option is incorrect. It reverses the purpose of each store. The online store is for real-time, low-latency lookups. The offline store is for batch training, historical analysis, and large-scale feature retrieval.

Use Amazon DynamoDB as a centralized feature repository, storing precomputed features for low-latency real-time access, and export snapshots to Amazon S3 for batch training: This option is technically possible but not the best answer. Amazon DynamoDB can provide low-latency key-value access, but it does not provide the MLOps-specific feature management, offline store integration, and SageMaker-native feature group capabilities of Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

Why SageMaker Feature Store online and offline stores fit this scenario.

The scenario requires feature reuse across projects.

It also requires support for real-time inference.

The same features must be available for batch training.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

Amazon SageMaker Feature Store provides two storage patterns for the same feature workflow.

The online store is used for low-latency feature retrieval.

This is the right store for real-time inference, such as retrieving customer, transaction, or device features during a live prediction request.

The offline store is used for historical feature data.

This is the right store for batch training, historical analysis, and large-scale dataset generation.

The offline store is backed by Amazon S3 and can be queried with services such as Amazon Athena.

Using both stores helps reduce training-serving skew.

Features are ingested and managed through a consistent feature store pattern instead of manually synchronizing separate systems.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Feature reuse: Centralize features in Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

Real-time inference: Use the online store.

Batch training: Use the offline store.

Historical data access: Query offline features from Amazon S3.

Training-serving consistency: Avoid manually synchronizing separate feature repositories.

Lower operational overhead: Use a managed SageMaker-native feature management service.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Feature reuse + real-time inference + batch training = Amazon SageMaker Feature Store with online and offline stores.

Remember:

Online store: Low-latency, single-record feature lookup for real-time inference.

Offline store: Historical feature storage for batch training and analytics.

Amazon S3: Backing storage for the offline store.

Amazon Athena: Can query offline store data.

Training-serving skew: Happens when training features differ from inference-time features.

Amazon DynamoDB: General-purpose key-value database, not a full ML feature store.

Manual S3 feature management: Higher operational overhead and greater consistency risk.

Official AWS references.

Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

Key exam terms: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store, online store, offline store, training-serving skew, feature reuse, real-time inference, batch training, point-in-time correctness.

question:
A public transportation authority, MetroTransit Services, needs to analyze large volumes of vehicle inspection and maintenance forms and identify important entities such as technician names, fault codes, and replacement parts.

These forms include both printed text and handwritten content.

The authority also needs to extract and categorize information to automate the documentation process and store the extracted metadata for further querying. Which combination of AWS services would BEST meet the organization's requirements?
options: Amazon Textract for extracting both printed and handwritten text, Amazon Comprehend for entity recognition, and Amazon S3 for storing the extracted metadata.
Amazon Rekognition for detecting text and images, Amazon Comprehend for analyzing the extracted text, and Amazon Aurora for storing and querying the structured data.
Amazon SageMaker for handwriting recognition, Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and Amazon Kendra for querying the extracted metadata.
Amazon Comprehend for entity extraction, Amazon Textract for analyzing images and text, and Amazon OpenSearch Service for indexing and querying the results.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests the ability to compose a purpose-built AWS AI/ML service pipeline for document intelligence.

It focuses on using Amazon Textract for document text extraction, Amazon Comprehend for NLP enrichment and entity recognition, and Amazon S3 for scalable metadata storage.

It is tied to the Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML) domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Amazon SageMaker for handwriting recognition, Amazon Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and Amazon Kendra for querying the extracted metadata: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker is a platform for building, training, and deploying custom ML models, but it is not the purpose-built service for extracting printed and handwritten text from documents. Amazon Kendra is used for enterprise search, not as the primary metadata storage layer for extracted structured data.

Amazon Comprehend for entity extraction, Amazon Textract for analyzing images and text, and Amazon OpenSearch Service for indexing and querying the results: This option is partially correct but not the best answer. Amazon Textract and Amazon Comprehend are relevant, but Amazon OpenSearch Service adds unnecessary operational overhead unless the scenario explicitly requires full-text search or search-cluster functionality.

Amazon Rekognition for detecting text and images, Amazon Comprehend for analyzing the extracted text, and Amazon Aurora for storing and querying the structured data: This option is incorrect. question:

The team is evaluating whether to use Amazon SageMaker's built-in algorithms instead of building custom models from scratch. Which of the following advantages do built-in SageMaker algorithms offer for this use case? (Select TWO.)

Built-in algorithms can only be used for simple tasks like linear regression and are not suitable for complex machine learning tasks.

question:
A mining and minerals company, OreVault Analytics, has developed a relatively small neural network model that completes a full training run in under two minutes.

The ML engineering team needs to perform hyperparameter tuning and must systematically guarantee complete coverage of the entire hyperparameter space  ensuring that every possible combination of the defined hyperparameter values is evaluated. Which hyperparameter search strategy is most suitable given these constraints?
options: Grid Search
Random Search
Hyperband
Bayesian Optimization
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests the ability to select the correct hyperparameter search strategy based on search-space size, training cost, and coverage requirements.

It focuses on choosing Grid Search when the hyperparameter space is small, training is inexpensive, and the requirement is to guarantee that every combination is evaluated.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Grid Search: This is the correct option. Grid Search evaluates every combination in a predefined hyperparameter grid. It is appropriate when the search space is small, training jobs are inexpensive, and exhaustive coverage is required.

Bayesian Optimization: This option is incorrect for this scenario. Bayesian Optimization is sample-efficient and useful when training jobs are expensive. It tries to find strong configurations with fewer trials, but it does not guarantee complete enumeration of all combinations.

Random Search: This option is incorrect. Random Search samples configurations randomly from the search space. It can work well in large or high-dimensional spaces, but it provides probabilistic coverage, not guaranteed exhaustive coverage.

Hyperband: This option is incorrect. Hyperband uses early stopping to allocate more resources to promising configurations and stop weaker ones early. It is useful for reducing compute cost, but it does not test every configuration fully.

Why Grid Search fits this scenario.

The scenario requires complete coverage of the hyperparameter space.

The training cost is low.

The number of combinations is small enough to evaluate exhaustively.

That points directly to Grid Search.

Grid Search systematically tests every combination from a predefined set of hyperparameter values.

Because it does not skip or sample configurations, it guarantees full coverage of the grid.

This is useful when the team wants certainty that every candidate configuration has been evaluated.

Other strategies optimize for different constraints.

Bayesian Optimization is better when each training job is expensive and the goal is to reduce the number of trials.

Random Search is better when the search space is large and only partial exploration is practical.

Hyperband is better when early stopping and resource efficiency matter more than full coverage.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Exhaustive coverage: Use Grid Search.

Small search space: Evaluate all combinations.

Low training cost: Full enumeration is practical.

No skipped configurations: Avoid random or probabilistic search.

No early stopping: Avoid Hyperband when every configuration must be evaluated.

SageMaker tuning strategy selection: Match the strategy to the cost and coverage constraints.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Small hyperparameter space + inexpensive training + guaranteed full coverage = Grid Search.

Remember:

Grid Search: Exhaustive evaluation of all predefined combinations.

Bayesian Optimization: Sample-efficient search for expensive training jobs.

Random Search: Random sampling for large or high-dimensional spaces.

Hyperband: Early stopping and resource-efficient search.

Exhaustive coverage: Strong signal for Grid Search.

Training cost: Determines whether full enumeration is practical.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning: Supports different search strategies for hyperparameter optimization.

Official AWS references.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning.

Key exam terms: Grid Search, Bayesian Optimization, Hyperband, Random Search, exhaustive coverage, hyperparameter tuning, Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning, early stopping.

question:
An education technology company, LearnPath Analytics, is using Amazon SageMaker Debugger to monitor and debug a deep learning model during training.

The model is designed to predict student dropout risk based on engagement and assessment data.

The team observes that the model's loss has plateaued and performance is no longer improving. They suspect the root cause is vanishing gradients propagating through the network.

Which of the following steps should the team take to diagnose and address this issue using SageMaker Debugger?
options: Use Amazon SageMaker Neo to compile and optimize the model for target hardware, which will also resolve gradient instability during training.
Increase the batch size in the training script so that gradient aggregation across more samples reduces the vanishing gradient effect.
Set up a custom rule in SageMaker Debugger to detect vanishing gradients and adjust the learning rate or change the optimizer accordingly.
Manually stop the training job, augment the dataset with additional training samples, and restart the job to resolve the vanishing gradient problem.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SageMaker Debugger and its ability to monitor training internals.

It focuses on detecting gradient-related training issues, such as vanishing gradients, and selecting the right training-time remediation strategy.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Increase the batch size in the training script so that gradient aggregation across more samples reduces the vanishing gradient effect: This option is incorrect. Increasing batch size can affect gradient estimate stability, but it does not directly solve vanishing gradients. Vanishing gradients are usually caused by deep network architecture, activation functions, and backpropagation behavior.

Use Amazon SageMaker Neo to compile and optimize the model for target hardware, which will also resolve gradient instability during training: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Neo optimizes trained models for inference on target hardware. It does not affect training-time gradient computation or resolve vanishing gradients.

Set up a custom rule in SageMaker Debugger to detect vanishing gradients and adjust the learning rate or change the optimizer accordingly: This is the correct option. Amazon SageMaker Debugger can monitor tensors such as gradients, weights, and activations during training. It supports built-in and custom rules for detecting issues such as vanishing gradients. Once detected, the team can adjust the learning rate, optimizer, or training strategy.

Manually stop the training job, augment the dataset with additional training samples, and restart the job to resolve the vanishing gradient problem: This option is incorrect. More data can help with generalization, but it does not directly fix vanishing gradients. The issue is related to training dynamics and gradient flow, not dataset size.

Why SageMaker Debugger with a vanishing gradient rule fits this scenario.

The scenario describes training instability.

The specific issue is vanishing gradients.

That means gradients become extremely small as they propagate backward through the network.

When this happens, earlier layers learn very slowly or stop learning effectively.

That points to Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

Amazon SageMaker Debugger can capture tensors during training.

These tensors can include weights, gradients, activations, and losses.

The service supports built-in rules and custom rules for detecting problematic training behavior.

For vanishing gradients, the team can use a built-in rule such as VanishingGradient or create a custom rule with smdebug.

After the issue is detected, the correct remediation is training-time adjustment.

Examples include changing the optimizer, tuning the learning rate, using learning rate scheduling, applying gradient clipping, or modifying architecture choices such as activation functions, normalization layers, or residual connections.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Detect training instability: Use Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

Monitor gradients: Capture tensor data during training.

Identify vanishing gradients: Use a built-in or custom rule.

Apply training-time remediation: Adjust learning rate, optimizer, or architecture.

Avoid inference-tool confusion: Do not use Amazon SageMaker Neo.

Avoid data-volume confusion: Do not solve gradient flow issues by simply adding more data.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Vanishing gradients + training instability + tensor monitoring = Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker Debugger: Monitors training internals such as tensors and system metrics.

VanishingGradient rule: Detects gradients that become too small.

smdebug: Library used for custom debugging rules and tensor analysis.

Learning rate adjustment: Valid remediation for training instability.

Optimizer change: Valid remediation when gradient behavior is poor.

Amazon SageMaker Neo: Inference optimization, not training debugging.

Data augmentation: Helps data coverage, not vanishing-gradient mechanics.

Official AWS references.

Use Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

Amazon SageMaker Debugger built-in rules.

Key exam terms: Amazon SageMaker Debugger, VanishingGradient rule, smdebug, custom rule, training instability, optimizer adjustment, learning rate scheduling, gradient clipping.

question:

The team stores raw sensor telemetry data  such as wafer inspection events and fabrication process interactions  in an Amazon S3 bucket.

They need to preprocess this data to remove duplicates, normalize numerical features, and encode categorical variables before model training. The preprocessing solution must scale automatically to accommodate continuously increasing data volumes and integrate natively with the SageMaker training workflow.

Which solution will most effectively meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Glue ETL jobs to preprocess the data, apply deduplication, normalization, and encoding transforms, and then load the transformed data into Amazon SageMaker for training.
Use Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs with a pre-built container for data preprocessing, and store the processed data back in Amazon S3.

explanation:

Use Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs with a pre-built container for data preprocessing, and store the processed data back in Amazon S3: This is the correct option. Use Amazon Athena to query the raw data and perform all preprocessing transformations using SQL, then export the processed dataset back to Amazon S3 for training: This option is incorrect. Amazon Athena is useful for querying data in Amazon S3 with SQL, but it is not a full ML preprocessing environment. It is not ideal for feature normalization, categorical encoding, or reusable ML preprocessing logic inside a SageMaker-centric pipeline.

Why SageMaker Processing Jobs fit this scenario.

The scenario requires scalable preprocessing.

The output must be prepared for model training.

The workflow is centered on Amazon SageMaker.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs.

Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs run preprocessing workloads in a fully managed environment.

They can use pre-built containers, such as containers for Scikit-learn or Spark, or custom containers when the team needs more control.

That output can then be consumed by Amazon SageMaker training jobs or orchestrated through Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.

This avoids managing an Amazon EMR cluster and avoids stitching together a separate ETL service when the preprocessing workload belongs directly inside the ML lifecycle.

This satisfies the key requirements:

ML preprocessing: Use Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs.

Managed execution: Avoid manual cluster management.

Pre-built containers: Use supported ML processing environments.

Custom logic support: Bring custom preprocessing code when needed.

S3 output storage: Store processed datasets in Amazon S3.

Native SageMaker integration: Connect preprocessing to training and pipeline orchestration.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

SageMaker-centric ML workflow + scalable preprocessing + minimal infrastructure management = Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs: Managed preprocessing, evaluation, and post-training analysis jobs.

Pre-built containers: Support common frameworks such as Scikit-learn and Spark.

Amazon S3: Common input and output storage layer.

Amazon SageMaker Pipelines: Can orchestrate processing, training, tuning, and registration steps.

AWS Glue: General-purpose ETL and data catalog workflows.

Amazon EMR: Distributed big data processing when Spark/Hadoop cluster capabilities are explicitly required.

Amazon Athena: SQL querying, not full ML preprocessing.

Official AWS references.

Amazon SageMaker Processing Jobs.

explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of the two-part setup required to activate Amazon SageMaker Profiler for CPU and GPU monitoring in a PyTorch training job.

It focuses on configuring profiling at both levels:

The Amazon SageMaker Estimator configuration.

The training script instrumentation.

It is tied to the Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Manually enable automatic SageMaker Profiler optimization in the SageMaker console to reduce memory overhead during training: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Profiler is not enabled through a one-click console optimization setting. It requires explicit programmatic configuration. It also observes resource usage; it does not automatically optimize memory overhead.

Define the profiler configuration in your SageMaker Estimator, specifying the duration of the profiling in seconds for the CPU and GPU: This is a correct option. The Amazon SageMaker Estimator must include a ProfilerConfig through the profiler_config parameter. This defines profiling behavior, such as the output location and system monitoring interval.

Use SageMaker Neo to compile the model for optimized CPU and GPU performance before the training job begins: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Neo compiles trained models for optimized inference on target hardware. It is not used to profile CPU and GPU utilization during training.

Configure SageMaker Profiler to automatically tune hyperparameters such as learning rate based on observed resource utilization data: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Profiler is an observability and diagnostics tool. It does not tune hyperparameters. Hyperparameter optimization is handled by Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning.

Import the necessary SageMaker Profiler modules and add start and stop profiling commands in the PyTorch training script: This is a correct option. The training script must import the required profiler modules and use profiling hooks such as start_profiling() and stop_profiling() to define the profiling window.

Why ProfilerConfig and script instrumentation fit this scenario.

The scenario requires CPU and GPU monitoring during a PyTorch training job.

That requires configuration in two places.

First, the Amazon SageMaker Estimator must define the profiler configuration.

This is done with ProfilerConfig.

The profiler configuration tells Amazon SageMaker where to store profiling data and how frequently to collect system metrics.

Second, the training script must be instrumented.

For a PyTorch job, the script needs the required Amazon SageMaker Profiler imports and profiling hooks.

The start_profiling() and stop_profiling() calls define the part of the training script that should be profiled.

Together, these two pieces allow Amazon SageMaker Profiler to collect system resource usage and framework-level training information.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Estimator-level setup: Configure ProfilerConfig.

Training script setup: Add profiler imports and start/stop hooks.

CPU and GPU visibility: Capture system resource usage.

PyTorch profiling: Instrument the framework training script.

S3 output storage: Store profiling artifacts in Amazon S3.

Avoid service confusion: Do not use Amazon SageMaker Neo or Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning for training profiling.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

SageMaker Profiler + PyTorch training job = ProfilerConfig in the Estimator + start/stop profiling hooks in the script.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker Profiler: Observes CPU, GPU, memory, and framework-level training behavior.

ProfilerConfig: Estimator-level configuration for profiling.

profiler_config: Estimator parameter used to enable profiler settings.

start_profiling() and stop_profiling(): Script-level hooks that define the profiling window.

Amazon SageMaker Neo: Compiles trained models for inference optimization.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning: Tunes hyperparameters, not profiling.

Profiler role: Diagnostics and observability, not automatic optimization.

Official AWS references.

Profile system resource usage with Amazon SageMaker Profiler.

question:
A data analyst at PrecisionForge Industries, an industrial manufacturing company, wants to extract meaningful insights from unstructured customer feedback stored in Amazon S3.

The insights must include the identification of key entities such as people, organizations, and locations mentioned in the feedback, as well as a determination of the overall sentiment expressed in each piece of feedback. Which combination of Amazon Comprehend features should the analyst use to achieve this goal?
options: Entity Recognition and Sentiment Analysis
Text Classification and Entity Recognition
Keyphrase Extraction and Sentiment Analysis
Topic Modeling and Keyphrase Extraction
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests the ability to map specific NLP requirements to the correct Amazon Comprehend features.

It focuses on selecting Entity Recognition when the requirement is to extract named entities, and Sentiment Analysis when the requirement is to determine the emotional tone of text.

It is tied to the Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML) domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Text Classification and Entity Recognition: This option is incorrect. Text Classification assigns documents to categories, but it does not provide sentiment scoring. Although Entity Recognition satisfies the named-entity extraction requirement, the sentiment requirement remains unmet.

Topic Modeling and Keyphrase Extraction: This option is incorrect. Topic Modeling discovers themes across a document corpus, and Keyphrase Extraction identifies important phrases. Neither feature extracts typed named entities and neither returns document sentiment.

Keyphrase Extraction and Sentiment Analysis: This option is partially correct but still incorrect overall. Sentiment Analysis satisfies the sentiment requirement, but Keyphrase Extraction does not identify typed named entities such as people, organizations, or locations.

Entity Recognition and Sentiment Analysis: This is the correct option. Entity Recognition extracts and classifies named entities from unstructured text. Sentiment Analysis determines whether the text is positive, negative, neutral, or mixed.

Why Entity Recognition and Sentiment Analysis fit this scenario.

The scenario has two requirements.

First, the system must extract named entities from unstructured text.

That points to Amazon Comprehend Entity Recognition.

Entity Recognition can identify entity types such as PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LOCATION, DATE, QUANTITY, and other supported entity categories.

Second, the system must determine the sentiment of the text.

That points to Amazon Comprehend Sentiment Analysis.

Sentiment Analysis returns labels such as POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, NEUTRAL, or MIXED, along with confidence scores.

Together, these two features satisfy both requirements.

Keyphrase Extraction is not enough because key phrases are not the same as typed named entities.

Text Classification is not enough because it assigns categories but does not provide sentiment.

Topic Modeling is not enough because it discovers themes across a corpus rather than extracting named entities and sentiment per document.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Named entity extraction: Use Entity Recognition.

Typed entity output: Identify people, organizations, locations, dates, and quantities.

Sentiment detection: Use Sentiment Analysis.

Unstructured text processing: Use Amazon Comprehend.

Avoid keyphrase confusion: Do not treat key phrases as named entities.

Avoid classification confusion: Do not use Text Classification when sentiment scoring is required.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Named entities + sentiment from unstructured text = Amazon Comprehend Entity Recognition + Sentiment Analysis.

Remember:

Entity Recognition: Extracts typed named entities.

Sentiment Analysis: Returns sentiment labels and confidence scores.

DetectEntities: API used for entity detection.

DetectSentiment: API used for sentiment detection.

Keyphrase Extraction: Finds important phrases, not typed entities.

Text Classification: Assigns categories, not sentiment.

Topic Modeling: Finds corpus-level themes, not per-document sentiment.

Official AWS references.

How Amazon Comprehend works.

Key exam terms: Amazon Comprehend, Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, DetectEntities API, DetectSentiment API, named entities, unstructured text, Keyphrase Extraction, Text Classification, Topic Modeling.

question:
A machine learning engineer at AeroVantage Systems, an aerospace and defense contractor, is setting up an isolated development environment to iteratively build, train, and deploy machine learning models using Amazon SageMaker.

The engineer requires a fully managed Jupyter notebook environment that eliminates manual infrastructure provisioning, comes with popular ML libraries such as TensorFlow and PyTorch pre-installed, and automatically persists all work to durable storage so that sessions can be resumed at any time without data loss. Which Amazon SageMaker feature BEST meets all of these requirements?
options: SageMaker Studio with JupyterLab spaces configured on a shared domain
SageMaker Notebook Instances
Amazon EC2 instance with a Deep Learning AMI and Jupyter notebook manually launched
SageMaker Training Jobs with a custom script entry point and interactive debugging enabled via SageMaker Debugger
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of interactive ML development environments in Amazon SageMaker.

It focuses on selecting Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances when the requirement is a fully managed, single-user Jupyter environment with pre-installed ML libraries and persistent storage.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

SageMaker Studio with JupyterLab spaces configured on a shared domain: This option is a strong distractor. Amazon SageMaker Studio provides managed Jupyter environments, but it is designed as a broader multi-user MLOps environment with domain, user profile, and shared storage configuration. That is more setup than needed for a single engineer who needs a simple managed notebook.

SageMaker Notebook Instances: This is the correct option. Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances provide fully managed Jupyter notebook environments with ML frameworks pre-installed and persistent Amazon EBS storage attached to the notebook instance.

Amazon EC2 instance with a Deep Learning AMI and Jupyter notebook manually launched: This option is incorrect. Amazon EC2 with a Deep Learning AMI can provide ML libraries and Jupyter, but the user must manage the instance, networking, updates, security groups, and Jupyter server configuration. It is not the lowest-overhead managed option.

SageMaker Training Jobs with a custom script entry point and interactive debugging enabled via SageMaker Debugger: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs run training workloads in managed containers. They are not designed to provide a persistent interactive Jupyter notebook environment.

Why SageMaker Notebook Instances fit this scenario.

The scenario requires an interactive notebook environment.

It is for an individual engineer.

The environment must be fully managed.

It must include common ML libraries.

It must also preserve notebooks and files across sessions.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances.

A notebook instance runs Jupyter on a managed ML compute instance.

AWS handles much of the infrastructure setup.

The environment includes commonly used ML frameworks and libraries through AWS-managed environments.

The notebook instance is backed by persistent Amazon EBS storage.

That means notebooks, scripts, and local files can remain available when the instance is stopped and started again.

This makes notebook instances a clean fit for individual experimentation, prototyping, and interactive ML development.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Interactive development: Use a managed Jupyter notebook.

Single-user environment: Use Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances.

Pre-installed ML libraries: Use AWS-managed notebook environments.

Persistent storage: Store notebooks and files on Amazon EBS.

Low operational overhead: Avoid manually configuring Jupyter on Amazon EC2.

Avoid platform mismatch: Do not use Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs for interactive notebook development.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Single-user managed Jupyter + pre-installed ML libraries + persistent storage = Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances: Managed Jupyter environment for ML development.

Amazon EBS: Persistent storage attached to notebook instances.

Pre-installed frameworks: Common ML libraries are available in managed environments.

Amazon SageMaker Studio: Broader collaborative MLOps environment.

Amazon EC2 Deep Learning AMI: More manual setup and infrastructure management.

Amazon SageMaker Training Jobs: Batch-style training execution, not an interactive notebook interface.

Amazon SageMaker Debugger: Training inspection and debugging, not a notebook environment.

Official AWS references.

Use Amazon SageMaker notebook instances.

Key exam terms: Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instances, fully managed Jupyter, pre-installed ML frameworks, Amazon EBS persistent storage, no infrastructure provisioning, single-user development environment, Amazon SageMaker Studio distractor, Deep Learning AMI.

In addition, they must capture custom operational metrics such as the number of active inference requests per second.

Which combination of AWS services and features is the MOST appropriate to satisfy both the standard and custom monitoring requirements with minimal operational overhead?
options: Enable AWS Config to track ECS task performance changes and set up Amazon CloudWatch Alarms for CPU and memory metric thresholds.
Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture ECS API calls and use Amazon EventBridge rules to forward CPU and memory metrics into Amazon CloudWatch.
Use AWS Lambda to regularly poll ECS task performance data and push CPU and memory metrics into Amazon CloudWatch for analysis.

What this question tests.

This question tests understanding of Amazon SageMaker as a fully managed, end-to-end machine learning platform.

It focuses on recognizing that Amazon SageMaker abstracts infrastructure management across data preparation, training, tuning, deployment, and monitoring.

It is tied to the Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows domain.

The concepts at a glance.

SageMaker simplifies the machine learning workflow by providing a fully managed service that handles data preparation, model training, and deployment without requiring manual server management: This is the correct option. Amazon SageMaker provides managed capabilities across the ML lifecycle, including data preparation, processing, training, tuning, deployment, and monitoring. Users do not need to manually provision or manage servers.

SageMaker exclusively assists in the model training phase; the company must use additional AWS services such as AWS Glue and Amazon ECS for data preparation and model deployment, respectively: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker is not limited to training. It includes services such as Amazon SageMaker Processing, Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler, Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, Amazon SageMaker Endpoints, and Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

SageMaker natively integrates with Amazon EC2 instances that must be manually provisioned and configured for each machine learning task, while SageMaker manages only the data preparation and monitoring layers: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker uses compute infrastructure under the hood, but users do not manually provision or configure Amazon EC2 instances for SageMaker-native training and deployment workflows.

SageMaker requires manual infrastructure setup — including server provisioning and scaling configuration — for model training jobs, but simplifies the deployment phase through managed real-time endpoints: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker manages infrastructure for both training and deployment. Training jobs automatically provision the requested compute, run the job, and release resources when complete.

Why SageMaker as a fully managed ML platform fits this scenario.

The scenario emphasizes a fully managed ML workflow.

It requires support across the machine learning lifecycle.

It also requires avoiding manual server management.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker.

Amazon SageMaker provides managed tools for data preparation, processing, model training, hyperparameter tuning, deployment, monitoring, and workflow orchestration.

For training jobs, Amazon SageMaker provisions the requested compute resources automatically.

After the job completes, it tears down the training infrastructure.

For deployment, Amazon SageMaker provides managed inference options such as real-time endpoints, asynchronous inference, serverless inference, and batch transform.

This allows teams to focus on ML workflows instead of managing servers, patching instances, configuring infrastructure manually, or building deployment platforms from scratch.

This satisfies the key requirements:

End-to-end ML lifecycle: Use Amazon SageMaker.

Fully managed infrastructure: Avoid manual server provisioning.

Managed training: Let Amazon SageMaker provision and terminate training resources.

Managed deployment: Use Amazon SageMaker inference options.

Operational monitoring: Use services such as Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

Workflow orchestration: Use Amazon SageMaker Pipelines when repeatable ML workflows are required.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Fully managed ML lifecycle + no server management = Amazon SageMaker.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker: Fully managed platform for building, training, deploying, and monitoring ML models.

Amazon SageMaker Processing: Managed data processing jobs.

Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler: Low-code data preparation and feature engineering.

Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning: Managed hyperparameter optimization.

Amazon SageMaker Endpoints: Managed inference hosting.

Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: Production model and data monitoring.

Official AWS references.

question:
A data scientist at NovaSoft Systems, a mid-size enterprise software vendor, is building a machine learning pipeline using Amazon SageMaker Pipelines. The pipeline includes data preprocessing, model training, and model registration steps.

The data scientist needs to ensure that hyperparameters and configuration values used during model training can be easily adjusted at execution time without modifying the pipeline definition itself, supporting rapid experimentation across multiple runs.

Which feature of SageMaker Pipelines should the data scientist use to achieve this requirement?
options: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
SageMaker Experiments
Pipeline Steps
Pipeline Parameters
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SageMaker Pipelines parameterization.

It focuses on using Pipeline Parameters when the same pipeline definition must support different runtime values, such as hyperparameters, dataset paths, or instance types, without redefining the pipeline.

It is tied to the Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Directed Acyclic Graph: This option is incorrect. The DAG defines the execution order and dependencies between pipeline steps. It controls workflow structure, but it does not provide runtime configuration injection.

Pipeline Steps: This option is incorrect. Pipeline Steps define individual units of work, such as ProcessingStep, TrainingStep, or RegisterModelStep. Steps can consume parameters, but they are not the mechanism for declaring runtime-overridable values.

Pipeline Parameters: This is the correct option. Pipeline Parameters let teams define named, typed variables in a Amazon SageMaker Pipeline. These values can be overridden when the pipeline execution starts, allowing reuse of the same pipeline definition across multiple runs.

SageMaker Experiments: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Experiments tracks and compares training runs, metrics, parameters, and artifacts. It supports experiment observability, but it does not inject runtime configuration into a pipeline.

Why Pipeline Parameters fit this scenario.

The scenario requires flexibility at execution time.

The team wants to reuse the same pipeline definition.

They need to change values such as dataset paths, hyperparameters, or instance types without editing the pipeline logic.

That points directly to Pipeline Parameters.

In Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, parameters are declared when the pipeline is defined.

Examples include ParameterString, ParameterInteger, and ParameterFloat.

These parameters can have default values.

When a new pipeline execution starts, the team can override those values through the AWS SDK, AWS CLI, or the Amazon SageMaker console.

This separates pipeline logic from runtime configuration.

The same compiled pipeline can support multiple experiments, environments, datasets, and training configurations.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Runtime flexibility: Use Pipeline Parameters.

Reusable pipeline definition: Avoid redefining the pipeline for each run.

Configurable training values: Pass hyperparameters, dataset paths, or instance types at execution time.

Typed variables: Use ParameterString, ParameterInteger, or ParameterFloat.

MLOps parameterization: Decouple configuration from orchestration logic.

Avoid observability confusion: Do not use Amazon SageMaker Experiments for runtime configuration injection.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Change values at execution time without modifying the pipeline definition = Pipeline Parameters.

Remember:

Pipeline Parameters: Runtime-overridable variables.

ParameterString: String input value for a pipeline execution.

ParameterInteger: Integer input value for a pipeline execution.

ParameterFloat: Floating-point input value for a pipeline execution.

DAG: Defines dependency and execution order.

Pipeline Steps: Define units of work.

Amazon SageMaker Experiments: Tracks and compares runs, not pipeline configuration injection.

Official AWS references.

Build and manage parameters in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.

Key exam terms: Pipeline Parameters, Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, ParameterInteger, ParameterString, runtime configuration, pipeline redefinition, MLOps parameterization, rapid experimentation.

question:
A regional banking institution, NorthBridge Financial, uses an AWS Lambda function triggered by Amazon SNS to preprocess customer transaction data before sending it to an Amazon SageMaker model for fraud detection.

The transaction data is subsequently stored in Amazon RDS for long-term analytics.

The bank requires that only valid transactions (based on a predefined schema) are passed to the SageMaker model, and that invalid transactions are logged and stored in Amazon S3 for further analysis  without degrading the performance or throughput of the fraud detection pipeline.

Which of the following solutions BEST fits the bank's requirements?
options: Set up an AWS Step Functions workflow to orchestrate schema validation, invoke AWS Lambda for processing valid transactions and sending them to SageMaker, and write invalid transactions to Amazon S3.

Use AWS Lambda to validate the schema of each transaction, send valid data to SageMaker for real-time inference, and forward invalid data to an Amazon SQS queue, which triggers a separate Lambda function to log and store it in Amazon S3.

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to preprocess and validate the data stream, invoke AWS Lambda to forward valid transactions to SageMaker, and redirect invalid transactions directly to Amazon S3 via a Firehose delivery stream.

Use a single AWS Lambda function to validate the schema of each transaction, invoke SageMaker for fraud detection on valid data, and write invalid transactions directly to Amazon S3 within the same function execution.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests event-driven ML inference architecture and asynchronous decoupling.

It focuses on using Amazon SQS to separate invalid-record handling from the low-latency fraud detection path that invokes a Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint.

It is tied to the Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Set up an AWS Step Functions workflow to orchestrate schema validation, invoke AWS Lambda for processing valid transactions and sending them to SageMaker, and write invalid transactions to Amazon S3: This option is not the best answer. AWS Step Functions is useful for complex workflow orchestration, branching, retries, and long-running processes, but it adds unnecessary orchestration overhead for a simple per-record validation and routing pattern.

Use AWS Lambda to validate the schema of each transaction, send valid data to SageMaker for real-time inference, and forward invalid data to an Amazon SQS queue, which triggers a separate Lambda function to log and store it in Amazon S3: This is the correct option. It keeps the critical inference path fast while moving invalid-record logging to an asynchronous, durable, independently scalable path.

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to preprocess and validate the data stream, invoke AWS Lambda to forward valid transactions to SageMaker, and redirect invalid transactions directly to Amazon S3 via a Firehose delivery stream: This option is incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is optimized for delivering streaming data to destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon OpenSearch Service. It is not the best fit for per-record schema validation and conditional routing to a real-time ML endpoint.

Use a single AWS Lambda function to validate the schema of each transaction, invoke SageMaker for fraud detection on valid data, and write invalid transactions directly to Amazon S3 within the same function execution: This option is incorrect. Writing invalid records to Amazon S3 synchronously inside the same function can increase latency and reduce throughput on the fraud detection path.

Why Lambda with SQS decoupling fits this scenario.

The pipeline is event-driven.

The input comes through Amazon SNS.

The valid records must be sent to a Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint for fraud detection.

The invalid records must still be preserved for logging, auditing, or later analysis.

These two paths have different latency requirements.

The valid-record path is latency-sensitive.

The invalid-record path is durability-sensitive but does not need to block real-time inference.

That points to asynchronous decoupling with Amazon SQS.

The first AWS Lambda function validates the schema.

If the record is valid, it invokes the Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint.

If the record is invalid, it sends the record to an Amazon SQS queue.

A separate AWS Lambda function is then triggered by the queue and writes the invalid record to Amazon S3.

This design keeps the fraud detection path fast.

It also gives the invalid-record path buffering, retry handling, durability, and independent scaling.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Low-latency inference: Keep valid records on the direct path to Amazon SageMaker.

Invalid-record durability: Store invalid events without blocking inference.

Asynchronous decoupling: Use Amazon SQS.

Independent scaling: Scale fraud detection and invalid-record persistence separately.

Schema validation: Perform validation before invoking the ML endpoint.

Separation of concerns: Keep inference logic separate from logging and persistence.

Avoid synchronous side effects: Do not write invalid records to Amazon S3 in the same critical execution path.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

SNS-triggered inference + valid records to Amazon SageMaker + invalid records stored separately + low latency = Amazon SQS decoupling with separate AWS Lambda functions.

Remember:

Amazon SNS: Event fanout and message notification service.

AWS Lambda: Good for lightweight event-driven validation and endpoint invocation.

Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint: Used for low-latency inference.

Amazon SQS: Buffers and decouples asynchronous work.

Amazon S3: Durable storage for invalid records, logs, or audit data.

AWS Step Functions: Better for complex orchestration, not simple decoupled routing.

Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose: Delivery service, not per-record ML routing logic.

Official AWS references.

Using AWS Lambda with Amazon SQS.

Invoke an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint.

Using AWS Lambda with Amazon SNS.

Key exam terms: Amazon SNS-triggered AWS Lambda, Amazon SageMaker real-time inference, Amazon SQS asynchronous decoupling, schema validation, fraud detection pipeline, separation of concerns, MLOps event-driven architecture, per-record conditional routing.

question:
A data science team at a large construction and engineering firm, BuildCore Solutions, is training a deep learning model that frequently encounters vanishing gradients and overfitting during the training process.

The team decides to integrate Amazon SageMaker Debugger to monitor and debug the model in real time, with the goal of resolving these issues before the model is promoted to a deployment pipeline.

Which of the following actions should the team take when configuring SageMaker Debugger for this task? (Select TWO.)
options: Configure a Debugger hook in the training script to capture and log tensors at defined collection intervals, providing real-time insights into model weights and gradients.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor on the training job to visualize and track CPU and GPU resource utilization and flag data quality violations that may cause overfitting.
Set up built-in or custom debug rules to monitor training metrics and automatically detect issues such as vanishing gradients or overfitting in real time.
Use SageMaker Experiments to register tensor snapshots as trial components, and configure automated stopping criteria based on gradient norms to prevent vanishing gradients.
Use SageMaker Profiler to automatically detect and correct hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size during training to mitigate vanishing gradients.
explanation:
What this question tests.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SageMaker Debugger for training-time diagnostics.

It focuses on using Debugger hooks to capture tensors during training and Debugger rules to detect issues such as vanishing gradients, overfitting, or abnormal weight updates.

It is tied to the ML Model Development domain.

The concepts at a glance.

Use SageMaker Profiler to automatically detect and correct hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size during training to mitigate vanishing gradients: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Profiler monitors system-level resource utilization, such as CPU, GPU, memory, and I/O. It does not automatically correct hyperparameters or analyze tensor-level issues such as vanishing gradients.

Set up built-in or custom debug rules to monitor training metrics and automatically detect issues such as vanishing gradients or overfitting in real time: This is a correct option. Amazon SageMaker Debugger provides built-in rules such as VanishingGradient, Overfit, and WeightUpdateRatio. Custom rules can also be created for domain-specific training diagnostics.

Enable SageMaker Model Monitor on the training job to visualize and track CPU and GPU resource utilization and flag data quality violations that may cause overfitting: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is used after deployment to monitor live endpoints. It does not diagnose training-time tensor behavior or training job overfitting.

Configure a Debugger hook in the training script to capture and log tensors at defined collection intervals, providing real-time insights into model weights and gradients: This is a correct option. A Debugger hook captures tensors such as weights, gradients, biases, activations, and losses during training and stores them for analysis.

Use SageMaker Experiments to register tensor snapshots as trial components, and configure automated stopping criteria based on gradient norms to prevent vanishing gradients: This option is incorrect. Amazon SageMaker Experiments tracks runs, parameters, metrics, and artifacts, but it does not perform real-time tensor-level anomaly detection or gradient-based stopping.

Why Debugger rules and hooks fit this scenario.

The scenario describes training-time problems.

The team needs to detect issues such as vanishing gradients and overfitting.

Those issues require visibility into tensors, gradients, weights, and training behavior while the job is running.

That points directly to Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

A Debugger hook captures tensor data during training.

It can collect values such as gradients, weights, biases, activations, and losses at configured intervals.

Those tensors are written to Amazon S3.

Debugger rules then evaluate the captured tensors.

Built-in rules can detect common training issues such as VanishingGradient, Overfit, and abnormal WeightUpdateRatio.

Custom rules can also be created when the team needs specialized checks.

This makes Amazon SageMaker Debugger the correct service for real-time training anomaly detection.

This satisfies the key requirements:

Training-time diagnostics: Use Amazon SageMaker Debugger.

Tensor capture: Configure a Debugger hook.

Gradient monitoring: Capture and inspect gradients during training.

Real-time anomaly detection: Use built-in or custom Debugger rules.

Overfitting detection: Use rules such as Overfit.

Vanishing gradient detection: Use the VanishingGradient rule.

Avoid service confusion: Do not use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor, Amazon SageMaker Experiments, or Amazon SageMaker Profiler for tensor-level training anomaly detection.

Exam tip.

The key exam signal is:

Training-time tensor analysis + gradients + overfitting or vanishing gradients = Amazon SageMaker Debugger hooks and rules.

Remember:

Amazon SageMaker Debugger: Captures and analyzes training tensors.

DebuggerHookConfig: Configures tensor collection for training jobs.

SMDebug SDK: Can be used inside training scripts for custom tensor capture.

VanishingGradient: Built-in Debugger rule for gradient issues.

Overfit: Built-in Debugger rule for overfitting detection.

Amazon S3: Stores captured tensors and Debugger outputs.

Amazon SageMaker Profiler: System/resource profiling, not tensor-level debugging.

Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: Post-deployment endpoint monitoring, not training-time debugging.

Official AWS references.

Debug and profile training jobs with Amazon SageMaker Debugger.
